Issued at 330 AM CDT Tue Aug 25 2026

All is quiet weather-wise across the area early this morning 
with temperatures in the 50s to lower 60s. Only concern is the 
potential for shallow ground fog development through daybreak, 
especially along river valleys and other typical fog prone low-
lying spots. Temperatures today will be slightly warmer than 
yesterday for some areas, in the upper 70s to lower 80s, as 
winds return to a southwesterly direction. The lake breeze will 
also mainly hug the Illinois lakeshore rather than surge farther
inland and allow warmer temperatures to reach areas closer to 
the lake this afternoon.

A closed upper low currently over southern Manitoba and 
Saskatchewan will very gradually drift southeast toward the 
northern Great Lakes today and tonight. An attendant cold front 
is then forecast to drift across the area through the day on 
Wednesday. Increasing low to mid level moisture ahead of the 
front will help set the stage for potential thunderstorm 
development into the afternoon and evening hours.

Prior to the front's arrival, there remains a signal for warm 
advective showers and non-severe thunderstorms developing in 
southwest Wisconsin and northwest Illinois late tonight which 
may drift southeast into portions of the area through early 
Wednesday morning. A stray shower or rumble of thunder may
linger through mid-morning across northern Illinois (20% 
chance).

While the center of the vort is expected to remain well to our 
north, steepening mid-level lapse rates along the trough axis 
paired with the increased low-level moisture ahead of the 
surface front should be sufficient for a pool of increasing 
instability (upwards of 2000-2500 J/kg MLCAPE) over portions 
east central Illinois and northwest Indiana Wednesday afternoon.
This paired with a 35-45kt 500mb jet overhead suggests any 
storms that develop will have the potential to become strong to 
severe. Storm mode will favor semi-discrete supercells initially
then potentially trending toward merging multi-cell clusters 
with southeast extent. Primary hazards include localized 
damaging winds, large hail, and localized downpours. While a 
tornado can't be ruled out with the strongest storms (owing to 
supercell mode paired with slight low-level hodograph 
curvature), it does appear that the locally higher potential is
just east of the area into north central Indiana.

Given the local area will be slightly displaced from the larger
vort (and mid-level forcing) to our north and northeast, 
questions remain regarding thunderstorm coverage with southwest 
extent along the front. Residual cloud cover or lingering 
showers through morning may also limit destabilization for at 
least portions of the area and especially west/northwest of the 
Chicago metro. The majority of CAM guidance does indicate there 
will be sufficient lift along the front to support storms 
initiating generally near the I-55 corridor in the afternoon 
with increasing coverage occurring along the front into east 
central Illinois and northern Indiana through early evening. 
Accordingly, the Storm Prediction Center has introduced a level 
2 out of 5 threat for severe weather for areas near and east of 
I-55. Expect some refinement to this area as the timing and 
location of storm initiation becomes more clear.

Looking ahead, a trailing weaker wave rounding the upper trough
over eastern Canada could support a few sprinkles on Thursday 
but expect mainly dry conditions with seasonably cool 
temperatures in the upper 70s to around 80 and comfortable 
humidity. Dry weather continues through the end of the week as 
upper ridging briefly expands east into the area Friday into 
Saturday paired with expansive surface high pressure. The upper 
levels then transition toward a more zonal flow pattern across 
the northern Plains and Upper Midwest which could bring a series
of disturbances across the broader region early next week 
paired with periodic shower and storm chances. Temperatures also
trend warmer with highs in the mid-upper 80s.

Petr
